say.text: Damascus, in the oasis of the Ghouta. Safar, 549 AH: April, 1154. The city is ruled by Mujir ad-Din Abaq; Nur ad-Din, lord of Aleppo, has laid siege to it.
Damascus lay between Nur ad-Din and the Franks of Ascalon, who laid a yearly tribute on it. Nur ad-Din feared that they would take it, and chose guile over force.

He sent Mujir ad-Din gifts and friendship. From time to time he warned him that one or another of his emirs had offered to betray the city, until Mujir ad-Din had dismissed or imprisoned the able ones.
And Nur ad-Din wrote to the young men of the city's urban guard, and they promised to hand the city to him.
Salah ad-Din, about sixteen years old, is a son of one of the emirs of Damascus and has come into the service of Nur ad-Din. He rides in the vanguard of Shirkuh.
The prince is shut up with his purse. The people and the guard are the gate, boy. Everything else is a wall.
My father is inside, uncle. He is one of this city's emirs.
Your father is a careful man. He will be where he is needed, and not where he is not.
I have never been in a battle.
Everyone has a first. Stand where I can see you, and do not go through a gate before you have asked who is behind it.
When Mujir ad-Din appealed to the Franks, offering them money and Baalbek, they began to gather their horse and foot to relieve him.
The guard has promised the East Gate. Find their captain: he will show himself when he knows it is us. Then it is a matter of reaching the wall before the Franks reach us.
